The perception that the consumer's classic vulnerability proves insufficient to explain asymmetries produced in digital ecosystems already appears clearly in recent literature, including in the field of electronic games. The problem, therefore, is not artificially created by the present thesis, but has already been identified by competing formulations that seek to name the aggravation of the consumer's fragility in platform environments. It is in this key that Azevedo and Torres work with the notion of “situational digital vulnerability”, pointing out that it may assume, among others, a “by captivity” form, linked to relationships that extend over time, and a “neuropsychological” one, caused mainly by the application of behavioral economics and gamification <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 8)</2>. The article becomes especially relevant because it brings this diagnosis to the universe of games, showing that, in the very empirical object privileged here, the need for supplementary categories to explain the intensification of vulnerability is already perceived. When dealing with Fortnite, the authors observe that situational digital vulnerability by captivity manifests itself “mainly through the consumer's submission to the platform, which holds the items acquired for use in the development of the game”, to which are added the multiplayer character and the formation of teams as factors of permanence in the environment <3>Torres</3><4>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 23)</4>. The merit of the reference lies precisely in showing that the problem was well perceived. The critical point, however, remains whether categories of this nature, strongly dependent on the environment and on the public affected, manage to isolate with sufficient precision the dogmatic mechanism of vulnerabilization. The aggravation of vulnerability in the digital environment need not be described only by broad labels of technological setting; it can be broken down into concrete factors of asymmetry produced by the very design of the platform. This is what makes the article by Azevedo and Torres useful for the critical review of the corpus. The authors describe contemporary digital architectures as structures that are “customizable, dynamic and governed by the analysis and interpretation of data”, capable of continuously collecting data, learning from user interactions and changing the environment “at any moment” to secure better results for the supplier through the exploitation of the consumer's vulnerabilities <5>Torres</5><6>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 15-16)</6>. Here one is no longer merely facing a generic technological scenario, but an operational arrangement that monitors, adjusts and influences conduct. This mechanical dimension appears even more clearly when the authors explain that prolonged use of the service increases the capacity to identify and target vulnerabilities, because continuous data collection allows the design to be adjusted to influence behavior, while captivity makes leaving the platform difficult and builds a kind of “situational monopoly” <7>Torres</7><8>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 11)</8>. Added to this, in the case of electronic games, is the presence of irregular rewards, sounds, colors and greater graphic immersion as factors of behavioral conditioning <9>Torres</9><10>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 21)</10>. The article thus has the merit of pointing out real mechanisms of aggravation of vulnerability, even though the chosen category remains strongly anchored in the broad frame of the “situational digital”. <11>↩</11>

The dogmatic operability of competing categories can also be tested by their capacity to generate concrete legal consequences, and not only by their descriptive aptitude. In this dimension, the formulation of Azevedo and Torres does not remain entirely on the sociological plane, since the authors seek to link it to specific protective responses within the consumer-law and constitutional system. This appears when they argue for the “hypervulnerability of the family unit” through equivalence to the child on the basis of art. 29 of the CDC, treating the family as a collectivity exposed to commercial practices which, although they initially reach minors, radiate effects to the whole family unit and weaken the exercise of parental authority <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 22)</2>. The same movement is seen when they associate the platform's practices with concrete duties to contain economic power and to provide integral protection to children and adolescents, calling on the State, society and the family to act in the face of the harm to healthy development produced by such dynamics <3>Torres</3><4>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 22- 23)</4>. The article, therefore, demonstrates some normative density and capacity to generate real protective consequences. Even so, the way these consequences are triggered reveals that the category remains very dependent on the public affected and on the specific context of incidence, which reinforces its usefulness as a qualified object of critical review, but also exposes the limits of its dogmatic stability as a general category of explanation. <5>↩</5>

The practical usefulness of categories such as “electronic”, “digital” or “technological vulnerability” appears more clearly when they are mobilized to describe real barriers produced by the compulsory digitalization of services, channels and procedures. At this point, the vocabulary allows concrete exclusions to be identified, above all when technology becomes an obstacle to access to justice, to communication or to the exercise of legally relevant positions <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 3)</2>. There is, therefore, some minimal normative yield: the duty of institutional adaptation, inclusion and accessibility. This connection is reinforced when the problem is brought close to the so-called “platform effect”, that is, the concentration of economic growth in a few scalable digital organizations <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 2)</4>. The text no longer speaks only of individual technical ignorance, but of structural asymmetries produced by platformized markets. Even so, it is precisely in this test of operability that the limit of the category appears most clearly. The center of the formulation remains tied to technological obstacles, digital environment and access to justice, and not to the rigorous identification of a dogmatically specific mechanism producing asymmetry within the consumer relation. The vocabulary is good for describing a context of exclusion and for justifying institutional accessibility responses. But for reconstructing, with greater precision, the duty breached, the factual basis, the required evidence and the appropriate remedy in digitally mediated consumer conflicts, it remains too atmospheric. <5>↩</5>

The critical review of recent literature reveals that the field is not organized only around the expression “digital vulnerability”, but also circulates through neighboring formulations such as “electronic vulnerability” and “technological vulnerability”. This terminological multiplication is already, in itself, a symptom of conceptual instability: the problem is clearly perceived, but there is still no sufficiently stable delimitation as to the name of the category or as to its scope. In one of these distinctions, it is argued that technological vulnerability would cover those unskilled in or excluded from the digital world, while digital vulnerability would reach subjects already inserted, in some way, in this scenario <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</2>. The critical consequence is clear: the recent competing vocabulary still presents mobile and poorly consolidated boundaries. The dispersion increases when several internal dimensions of this phenomenon are proposed, such as technological, technical, informational, algorithmic and neural or psychological-behavioral vulnerabilities <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</4>. The field shows sensitivity to the problem, no doubt, but also reveals a certain classificatory inflation. The picture becomes even more revealing when specific labels appear, such as the so-called “vulnerability by manipulation”, associated with gamification and training on digital platforms, including in gig economy contexts <5>Maia</5><6>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</6>. Here the material is valuable precisely because it shows the current state of the literature: fertile, intuitive, sensitive to new asymmetries, but semantically dispersed and oscillating between environment, technique, behavior, algorithm and exclusion from access. It is precisely this scenario that reinforces the need for the conceptual refinement undertaken by the present thesis. <7>↩</7>

The circulation of the expression “digital vulnerability” in fields other than consumption reinforces the perception that it is relevant, current and serious terminology, but semantically broad and dogmatically unstable. In the debate on access to justice, it appears associated with a multifaceted phenomenon ranging from the lack of physical access to the internet and to adequate devices to the absence of minimal digital skills for the use of technologies, with especially severe incidence on the elderly, people with low schooling and socially disadvantaged groups <1>Simões</1><2>(Simões, 2024, p. 79)</2>. The term is mobilized to name a structural condition of exclusion and difficulty of insertion into technologically mediated environments, and not a more delimited legal mechanism of relational asymmetry. This same key is reinforced when the problem is described in terms of barriers to access to justice: even with the gradual expansion of internet access, exclusions persist linked to the precariousness of the connection and to the insufficiency of technical skills, factors that become concrete obstacles to the use of institutionally digitalized channels <3>Simões</3><4>(Simões, 2024, p. 83)</4>. In this frame, so-called digital vulnerability appears as a new obstacle to access, adding to the classic barriers already identified <5>Simões</5><6>(Simões, 2024, p. 86)</6>. The vocabulary describes well a structural scenario of exclusion, but does so at a broad, environmental and transversal level, proving less precise for guiding attribution and evidence within the CDC. <7>↩</7>

The polysemy of the expression “digital vulnerability” appears even more clearly when it is presented as a new general layer of vulnerability linked to the growth of technological means and to the need for continuous adaptation to an entirely digitalized social life <1>Simões</1><2>(Simões, 2024, p. 69)</2>. The term already emerges, in this framing, less as a delimited dogmatic tool and more as the name of a general condition produced by a comprehensive sociotechnical transformation. This semantic openness expands even further when digital vulnerability is described as a state of predisposition to risk in cyberspaces, favoring inequities, power asymmetries, diminutions of citizenship and violations of privacy and informational self-determination, and is even brought close to the idea of socio-spatial vulnerability <3>Simões</3><4>(Simões, 2024, p. 79-80)</4>. Added to this is the recognition that the problem takes on diverse strands and frequently overlaps with other situations of vulnerability, in intersection with income, gender and race <5>Simões</5><6>(Simões, 2024, p. 80)</6>. The point is very useful here because it shows both the strength and the limit of the competing vocabulary: it sensitively captures a complex environment of exclusions, but tends to function as a broad category of context, less able to isolate the central legal mechanism of asymmetry that the thesis intends to delimit. <7>↩</7>

The critique of the literature on “digital vulnerability” cannot rest on the trivial fact that many consumer relations today unfold in technically complex contexts; that alone does not yet produce a dogmatic category. What matters, for consumer law, is to verify whether the formulation identifies a mechanism of functional opacity capable of compromising the consumer's understanding, choice and practical self-determination for the benefit of the supplier. It is exactly in this key that the passage mobilized by Wada <1>(2016)</1> offers a more solid criterion. In citing Benjamin, the text shows that, in mass and technically complex operations, the legally relevant datum lies not in the technology itself, but in the supplier's exploitation of the informational asymmetry of the “lay subject”. The problem arises when, faced with consumers not initiated in “complex technical, commercial, financial or tax transactions and operations”, the supplier takes advantage of the “weakness or ignorance of the consumer” to impose the opportunistic logic of “if it sticks, it sticks” <2>Wada</2><3>(Benjamin apud Wada, 2016, p. 193-194)</3>. This makes it possible to assess whether the literature on “digital vulnerability” really isolates an operable informational failure, marked by noise, opacity and the exploitation of ignorance, or whether it merely names, loosely, the technological scenario in which the relation takes place. The usefulness of Ricardo Morishita Wada's thesis, at this point, lies in allowing the consumer's informational vulnerabilization to be described through concrete mechanisms, and not through vague abstractions. Although the work does not fix “noise” or “functional opacity” as autonomous nominal categories, it precisely describes equivalent phenomena by showing that information can be formally provided and, at the same time, materially degraded in its function of clarification, comparison and decision. This can be seen, for example, when the structure of the offer reduces transparency and makes comparability unfeasible. In dealing with packages of banking products and services, Wada observes that the aggregation of multiple items “reduces price transparency”, hindering the comparison of offers, and that it was “very difficult for the consumer to compare the benefit packages offered by banks” <4>Wada</4><5>(Wada, 2016, p. 168)</5>. The information exists, but its form of presentation neutralizes its practical usefulness. The same logic appears when the author deals with the precariousness of the channel and the informational deficit as concrete instruments for exploiting vulnerability, noting that the “precariousness of verbal information may compromise the consumer's understanding” and proves incompatible with the regime of transparency, information and balance required by the CDC <6>Wada</6><7>(Wada, 2016, p. 213-214)</7>. In this key, noise, functional opacity and informational inadequacy cease to be convenient metaphors and come to designate concrete ways in which defective communication compromises understanding, comparability and practical freedom of choice. <8>↩</8>

The expression “digital vulnerability” will not be adopted here because, although it has descriptive usefulness, it delivers little dogmatic yield. It names the environment in which the injury occurs, but does not isolate the legally relevant mechanism of the asymmetry. The “digital” functions, in this vocabulary, as a marker of scenario, and not as an operator of attribution. This may be enough to indicate that there is specificity in technology-mediated consumption, but it does not suffice to guide, with precision, the passage from fact to normative consequence. The problem is not merely semantic. It is methodological. A concept, to be legally useful, must cut reality so as to make the conflict tractable, stabilizing what <1>p. 585</1> matters for duty, evidence, unlawfulness and remedy. When the category only describes the environment and not the mechanism, its yield for decidability is low <2>Jr.</2><3>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 81; p. 83])</3><4><5>656</5></4>.

This requirement of delimitation is not terminological fussiness. Legal dogmatics operates by functional simplification, and not by total description of the social world. Its work is to produce operational concepts that allow the conflict to be brought back to the necessary measure of its tractability. Categories too closely attached to the scenario tend to fail precisely where the law most needs them, because they retain descriptive breadth and lose the capacity to qualify the fact in terms of attribution and consequence. It is precisely for this reason that the expression “digital vulnerability” proves insufficient. It refers to a diffuse field of risks and asymmetries, but does not clarify, with sufficient sharpness, which form of vulnerabilization is at stake or how that form should be translated into duties and protective responses <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 108; p. 247])</2><3><4>657</4></3>.

The difficulty becomes more evident when one observes the recent doctrinal use of the label. “Digital vulnerability” may designate, depending on the context, technical-operational fragility, informational deficit, behavioral manipulation, infrastructure dependence, algorithmic <1>p. 586</1> opacity, technological exclusion or platform-mediated economic asymmetry. The result is an aggregating but poorly disciplined concept. It manages to gather in a single frame real contemporary phenomena, linked to the consumer journey, data protection, digital advertising, <2>profiling</2> and abusive practices in an informationally intensive market <3>Palmeira</3><4>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 167; p. 17)</4><5><6>658</6></5>. The problem is that, by condensing many different layers of risk, the expression ceases to indicate which of them matters legally in each case. Instead of cutting the problem, it accumulates it. And, when the category accumulates too much, evidence is dispersed and the remedy oscillates between excessive abstraction and casuistry.

This deficit is especially sensitive on the plane of legal technique. A concept does not serve only to describe a socially worrying situation. It must offer a normative form stable enough for one to say what must be proven, which duty was strained or breached and which consequence is adequate to the case. The empirical datum, by itself, does not automatically enter the universe of law. Its relevance depends on insertion into a normative structure that gives it intelligibility and operability. There is no raw legal fact. There is fact legally filtered by a normative form capable of converting it into a criterion of practical discipline <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 168; p. 96)</2><3><4>659</4></3>. It is for this reason that “digital vulnerability” proves weak. The expression names a state of affairs, but does not offer by itself the bridge between that state of affairs and the normative judgment that should follow from it.

<1>p. 587</1> This same critique can be formulated in another way. The legislator and the jurist do not act as sociologists who merely portray phenomena. They start from what is to determine what ought to be, associating legally relevant consequences with the conduct provided for. A category that remains on the descriptive plane, attached to the technical climate of the problem, does not fulfill this function well. The use of broad labels tends to produce the language of an era without disciplining the reconstruction of the relevant factual basis. Thus, it is not enough to recognize that the injury occurs in a digital medium. It must be converted into a normatively filtered category, able to guide judgments of lawfulness, duties of conduct and attributable consequences <2>Reale</2><3>(Reale, 2001, p. 32; p. 189)</3><4><5>660</5></4>.

This insufficiency also appears clearly in other competing vocabularies. The recent proliferation of expressions such as “electronic”, “virtual”, “digital” or “technological vulnerability” already reveals the perception that there is a new problem, but also the difficulty of naming it with sufficient precision. Such formulas are useful for indicating the scenario in which the difficulty emerges, especially when technology operates as an obstacle to access to justice, to understanding or to the exercise of legal positions<1><2>661</2></1>. But they remain very close to the technical frame of the problem and less able to identify the controllable legal <3>p. 588</3> mechanism of the asymmetry <4>Maia</4><5>(Maia, 2023, p. 3-4)</5><6><7>662</7></6>. They help to say where the problem happens. They say less about how it is produced in legally relevant terms.

For this reason, this discussion adheres to the expression “semiotic vulnerability”. The category aims at a mechanism, not a scenario. The central point lies not in the fact that the relation occurs in a digital medium, but in the way signs, discourses, interfaces and framings organize expectation, understanding, adherence, perception of value, perception of risk and perception of frustration. Language does not operate as ornament. It functions as an institutional technique of power. The legally relevant problem becomes the unequal administration of meaning, that is, the way the platform organizes the conditions of intelligibility of the consumption experience itself. It is in this key that signification can be analyzed as an instrument of social control, of normalization and of production of consensus, and not merely as a neutral vehicle of information <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2><3><4>663</4></3>.

This formulation has the advantage of shifting the gaze from the descriptive surface to the structure that produces legal effects. The focus ceases to fall on the technological environment itself and comes to fall on the socially operative production of meanings that conditions the way the experience will be lived, accepted and reproduced. Languages and discourses are not limited to transmitting informative content. They produce normative resonances, legitimize arrangements and <1>p. 589</1> generate effects of unquestionability over certain modes of functioning. Hence the pertinence of abandoning environmental labels in favor of categories that isolate the effective mechanism of production of meaning <2>Warat</2><3>(Warat, 1984, p. 15; p. 47)</3><4><5>664</5></4>.

This methodological shift can be reinforced by a restricted parallel. Critical categories lose density when they are lowered to the environment, the medium or the scenario in which they manifest themselves. The problem lies not in the technical medium itself, but in the social relation mediated by it. When a category comes to name only the context and not the mechanism, it retains intuitive force and loses operative force. The same risk occurs with “digital vulnerability”. The reference to the digital tends to indicate the technological environment of the injury, but not necessarily the specific form of production of the legally central asymmetry. The shift to “semiotic vulnerability” seeks to avoid precisely this lowering <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, p. 27; p. 31; p. 120)</2><3><4>665</4></3>.

In the IOC regime, this terminological choice is not only more precise; it is more useful. The platform does not merely provide information. It administers the showcase, the store, events, metrics, signals of rarity, promises of equivalence, narratives of value and the very framings through which the consumer perceives what was acquired. The relevant asymmetry is not merely a lack of data. It is the unequal administration of the meaning of the object consumed. In environments like these, expectation, consent, perception of value and perception of frustration are modulated by <1>p. 590</1> language and by design. Semiotic vulnerability makes it possible to name exactly this plane of incidence, without falling into subjectivism or environmental generalities.

This choice also produces an operational gain. It reorganizes the duty to inform in a qualitative, not quantitative, key. It is not enough to ensure formal access to data. Information must be correct, clear, precise and conspicuous, without excess, dispersion or barriers that compromise its practical usefulness for the consumer's decision. When communication appears transparent while producing material opacity, the problem lies not only in omission, but in the way the meaning of the relation is organized. The requirement ceases to be “more information” and becomes information able to guide decision, understanding and adequate use of the product or service. This is the point that allows the passage from the environmental label to the normative reconstruction of the mechanism.

The goal is to reach an applicable and minimally reliable discipline. The substitution of “semiotic vulnerability” for “digital vulnerability” makes the passage from fact to legal consequence more controllable. The duty to inform can be reconstructed as a requirement of adequacy and decisional usefulness, and not as a mere volume of data. Advertising becomes controllable by criteria of ambiguity, relevant omission, identification and truthfulness. Transparency ceases to be a showcase word and comes closer to a requirement of institutional verifiability. And the architecture of supply can be qualified, where appropriate, not merely as the context of the abuse, but as its very structured form of production. The gain is not aesthetic. It is dogmatic. The category better delimits the mechanism, better disciplines the evidence and better prepares the remedy.

The substitution of the expression "digital vulnerability" stems from a requirement of dogmatic operability. In legal discourse, it is not enough for a category to name, in broad terms, a technological environment marked by asymmetries and opacities; it must allow the legally relevant problem to be delimited, criteria of attribution to be stabilized and the passage to duty, unlawfulness, evidence and normative consequence to be guided. In this key, dogmatics is not organized to describe reality exhaustively, but to select, among its multiple aspects, what matters for the decision. As Ferraz Jr. observes, "unlike zetetic theories, dogmatic ones, concerned with the decidability of conflicts, do not take care to be logically rigorous in the use of their concepts and definitions, for to them what matters is not the relation with the phenomena of reality (describing the phenomena), but rather making a cut in reality, isolating the problems that are relevant for decision-making and diverting attention from the others" <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 81])</2>. For this reason, an overly broad expression may even have descriptive yield, but remain legally weak if it does not delimit the specific mechanism of vulnerabilization or the form of its normative incidence. It is at this point that the critique of the formula "digital vulnerability" holds, since its breadth tends to name a scenario without stabilizing, with sufficient sharpness, the legally central asymmetry. The problem, thus, is not one of empirical truth, but of dogmatic yield, since, as the author records, "its problem is not properly a question of truth, but of decidability" <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 83])</4>. <5>↩</5>

The refusal of excessively broad categories is also justified because legal dogmatics only makes the conflict tractable when it brings it back to a technically controllable plane. It is not the whole environment that enters legal reasoning, but only the delimitation necessary for its normative qualification and for its decision. Ferraz Jr. highlights this closure by stating that dogmatics operates by functional simplification of reality, producing "operational concepts" able to make the technical handling of the problem feasible <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 108])</2>. Expressions too closely attached to the scenario, although intuitively strong, may fail precisely where the law most needs them, especially in organizing the fact in terms of attribution, evidence and consequence. The insufficiency of "digital vulnerability" shows in this respect. The expression refers to a diffuse field of risks and asymmetries, but does not indicate with sufficient precision what the legally relevant mechanism is or how it should be translated into duties and protective responses. In a convergent sense, Ferraz Jr. observes that concrete conflicts, even when laden with multiple social, economic and political dimensions, only become legally tractable when they are brought back to the necessary measure of their decidability, and not faced "in all their concrete extension, but to the extent necessary for their decidability with a minimum of social disturbance" <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 247])</4>. It is this criterion that supports, here, the preference for a more delimited and controllable category. <5>↩</5>

The notion of vulnerability in the digital environment has real descriptive usefulness because it manages to gather, in a single frame, contemporary risks linked to the consumer journey, data protection, digital advertising and informational opacity. In this sense, the digital market is marked by growing difficulties in ensuring transparency in marketing practices based on monitoring, profiling and targeting of messages, as well as opacity in testing processes, use of <1>dark patterns</1>, insufficiency of consent as a legitimating basis and recurrence of security incidents involving personal data <2>Palmeira</2><3>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 167)</3>. The category thus clearly captures a contemporary ecosystem of risks and asymmetries. This aggregating character thickens when hypervulnerability is associated with the consumer's simultaneous position as addressee of market practices, as raw material of the marketing system and as product traded among its members, to which are added informational asymmetry and the widening of abusive practices founded on the prediction and manipulation of the consumer journey <4>Palmeira</4><5>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 17)</5>. <6>↩</6>

The refusal of the expression “digital vulnerability”, at this point, stems from an elementary methodological requirement: a legally useful concept cannot be limited to describing an environment, but must offer a normative form capable of converting social data into an operable criterion of attribution, evidence, duty and consequence. In Miguel Reale, the empirical datum, by itself, does not automatically enter the legal universe; its relevance depends on insertion into a normative structure that gives it intelligibility and operability. For this reason, the mere reference to the “digital” may even name a technical or historical scenario, but remains insufficient when it does not stabilize the legally relevant mechanism that explains the injury or guides the system's response. As the author states, “one cannot speak of Law, in the full sense of this word, without encompassing its essential moment of normativity, for social facts are only legal when inserted in a normative context” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 168)</2>. In a convergent sense, the legal norm corresponds to the “moment of integration of a class of facts according to an order of values”, and cannot be understood without simultaneous reference to these two poles, which it “dialectically integrates in itself and surpasses” <3>Reale</3><4>(Reale, 2001, p. 96)</4>. The broad label of “digital vulnerability” proves dogmatically loose, since it points to a context, but does not convert, by itself, social experience into a sufficiently precise legal criterion. <5>↩</5>

The critique of categories that remain on the merely descriptive plane finds direct support in Miguel Reale. For the author, legal construction is not satisfied with the mere observation of a state of affairs, because Law does not operate as a neutral description of social reality, but as a normative elaboration capable of transforming the empirical datum into a criterion of practical discipline. For this reason, the legislator does not act “in the manner of the sociologist”, limiting himself to portraying facts as they are; on the contrary, he starts from what is to determine what ought to be, associating legally relevant consequences with the conduct provided for in case of observance or violation of the norm <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 32)</2>. It is precisely this disciplined passage from fact to norm that prevents the legal concept from dissolving into an impressionistic label or mere language of an era. In this key, broad categories that only name contexts or environments fail when they cannot stabilize a legally relevant fact-type. Reale is explicit in stating that “one cannot speak of a legal fact except to the extent and insofar as it is inserted in a normative structure”, which is why “there is no raw fact in Law” <3>Reale</3><4>(Reale, 2001, p. 189)</4>. <5>↩</5>

When technology comes to be treated as an obstacle to access, to understanding or to the exercise of legal positions, the methodological risk lies in converting this finding into an overly broad category. The vocabulary of “electronic vulnerability” illustrates this: it allows real situations of exclusion or difficulty produced by the technological environment to be named, but tends to operate more as a description of context than as a dogmatic instrument of attribution. The focus remains on the fact that technological transformation can vulnerabilize and exclude, as occurs with subjects cut off from access to justice in scenarios of electronic proceedings, Online Courts, Justice 4.0, Justice 5.0 and ODR platforms <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 7)</2>. This formulation has real descriptive merit, but its explanatory force rests mainly on the idea of technological obstacle, and not on the finer identification of the legal mechanism that turns this barrier into a controllable asymmetry within a regime such as that of the CDC. The category points to the context of exclusion, but does not stabilize, with the desirable sharpness, the specific form in which the injury is produced. This becomes even more evident when the problem is inserted into the broad horizon of Society 5.0, the 4th Industrial Revolution and its systemic impacts on access, requiring special attention to the so-called technologically vulnerabilized <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 5)</4>. The synthesis of the so-called sixth renewal wave of access to justice confirms this design: it is presented as a field devoted to the analysis and mitigation of technology as an obstacle to a just legal order <5>Maia</5><6>(Maia, 2023, p. 7)</6>. The vocabulary helps to name the barrier, but remains short of explaining, with sufficient precision, the legal mechanism of the asymmetry. <7>↩</7>

The recent proliferation of labels such as “electronic”, “digital”, “virtual” or “technological vulnerability” already reveals, by itself, an important methodological difficulty: the field perceives that there is a new problem, but still oscillates in how to name it. These expressions have descriptive usefulness for indicating that certain asymmetries emerge in a technically mediated environment, but they tend to remain very close to the scenario in which the injury occurs, and less able to identify, with dogmatic sharpness, the legally relevant mechanism of vulnerabilization. It is in this sense that one speaks of “cyber or electronic vulnerability”, also designated as virtual, technological or digital vulnerability, when technology comes to function as an obstacle to access to justice <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 3)</2>. This feature is reinforced when the terminological dispute itself revolves around the greater or lesser vocabulary coverage of “digital” or “electronic”, that is, around the name most apt to cover the technical environment, and not around the most adequate category for individualizing the legally controllable factual basis. When it is recorded that “electronic” could be an even broader term, since it also reaches digital phenomena, it becomes even more visible how much the axis of the formulation remains centered on the technological frame of the problem <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 3-4)</4>. The category comes to name the technical climate of the injury, but not necessarily its mechanism. The same occurs when technological vulnerability is described as the individual's technical, informational, material or organizational limitation in dealing with information and communication technologies <5>Maia</5><6>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</6>. It helps to say where the problem happens and in what kind of scenario it intensifies, but still offers less precision for reconstructing, in a consumer-law key, duty, evidence, attribution and remedy. <7>↩</7>

The refusal of the expression “digital vulnerability”, at this point, can be deepened with Luis Alberto Warat because his semiology of power allows the focus to shift from the mere technical environment to the effectively relevant mechanism of production of subjection. The problem lies not in the “digital” taken as a generic scenario, but in the way signs, discourses and communicational framings organize understanding, expectation and adherence. Warat is explicit in stating that signification must be analyzed “as an instrument of social control”, “as a normalizing and disciplinary strategy of individuals”, “as a formula producing consensus” and “as persuasive power provoking effects of verisimilitude over the material conditions of social life” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>. The decisive point, therefore, is not technology itself, but the semiotic work that transforms certain conditions of power into an appearance of normality, validity and inevitability. In this key, a more precise legal category must aim at the mechanism of unequal intelligibility and semiotic capture, and not merely at the fact that the relation occurs in a digital environment. <3>↩</3>

Warat also offers a useful basis for justifying a legal category centered on mechanism, and not on scenario, because his reflection on language shifts the gaze from the descriptive surface to the socially operative production of effects of meaning. For the author, languages are not limited to the informative content they apparently transmit; they engender “significant and normalizing resonances of social practices”, inserting themselves into a deeper dynamic of “social production of meanings” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 15)</2>. This makes it possible to understand that the legally relevant problem lies not only in identifying the technical context in which the relation occurs, but in grasping how signification organizes in advance the intelligibility of experience and conditions the way it will be lived, accepted and reproduced. In a convergent sense, Warat observes that pragmatic analysis makes it possible to articulate functions such as “persuasion, legitimation, anticipation”, showing how certain discourses produce an “effect of unquestionability and reality over knowledge” <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</4>. Hence the pertinence of abandoning broad and environmental labels in favor of categories that isolate the effective mechanism of production of meaning. <5>↩</5>

Critical categories lose density when they are lowered to the environment, the medium or the scenario in which they manifest themselves. The warning appears clearly in the formulation according to which the spectacle is not to be confused with a set of images or with its technical means of diffusion, but consists in a social relation mediated by images <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, p. 27)</2>. For this reason, its reduction to the mass media corresponds only to the apprehension of its most visible superficial manifestation, and not of the structural mechanism that the category intends to describe <3>Debord</3><4>(Debord, 2013, p. 31)</4>. The same methodological reasoning allows the refusal of formulations that, although intuitively expressive, end up naming only the scenario in which the injury occurs. The risk is to retain descriptive force and lose dogmatic operability, because the category comes to point to context without stabilizing, with sufficient sharpness, the relevant factual basis, the strained duty, the required evidentiary standard and the corresponding legal consequence. The critique of the reduction of the spectacle to the “media-related”, precisely because it brings it back to a mere instrument and erases the social logic that the category sought to denounce, reinforces this methodological caution <5>Debord</5><6>(Debord, 2013, p. 120)</6>. Analogously, the expression “digital vulnerability” tends to become impoverished when it describes the technological environment without isolating the specific form of production of the legally relevant asymmetry. The shift to “semiotic vulnerability”, thus, does not stem from a vocabulary preference, but from the search for a category more apt to identify the effective mechanism of vulnerabilization, located in the unequal administration of meaning, of expectation, of the perception of risk, of the intelligibility of the offer and of the conditions of contestation. <7>↩</7>

In consumer relations, the problem of information was never merely quantitative. Contract, offer, interface and rules are forms of language, and it is through them that the market organizes expectation, adherence, comparison and resistance. For this reason, a relevant part of contractual injustice does not arise from the pure and simple absence of data, but from the way legally relevant meaning is produced, distributed and withheld. In a platform environment, the consumer may receive texts, dialog boxes, links, policies and notices in abundance and, even so, remain outside the real reach of understanding of what he accepts. It is on this plane that semiotic vulnerability becomes intelligible under its communicational aspect. The law faces not merely a failure of information, but a regime of communication that defines who manages to understand, who manages to compare and who manages to contest.

The CDC already contains the normative core of this problem. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information<1><2>681</2></1>. This means that the technical complexity of supply does not authorize the supplier to hide behind indecipherable vocabulary, documentary cascades or communicational architectures that deliver words and withhold meaning. Likewise, consumer contracts do not bind the consumer when he is not given a real opportunity of prior knowledge of the content, nor when they are drafted in a way that hinders the understanding of their meaning and scope<3><4>682</4></3>. The decisive point, therefore, lies not in proving that “the text was there”, but in assessing whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms.

<1>p. 602</1> This conclusion requires recognizing that language is not a neutral vehicle. Normative, contractual and institutional texts operate as techniques of production of selective intelligibility. They do not merely inform; they stabilize meanings, distribute access to significance and filter in advance the possible readings. Strictly speaking, contract and interface are not transparent containers of data, but institutional forms of organization of meaning. Legal and regulatory language is always crossed by strategic, ideological and pragmatic factors, which is why the problem of consent cannot be reduced to the physical availability of the statement. The consumer may receive the text, click, accept and even repeat its terms without effectively reaching its practical intelligibility<2><3>683</3></2>.

This point deepens when one perceives that the coherent organization of discourse also silences problems, excludes uncomfortable readings and stabilizes a previously controlled semantic frame. The appearance of univocity, closure and naturalness of the contractual text is not necessarily a sign of neutrality. Often, it functions precisely as a mechanism of communicational subjection. What is at stake is not only what the text expressly says, but the way it defines the field of the sayable, the comparable and the contestable<1><2>684</2></1>. On platforms, this is especially important, because contractual language <3>p. 603</3> does not come alone. It acts together with interface, adhesion flow, selective highlighting of information, placement of links and visual framings that guide the consumer to accept before understanding.

For this reason the asymmetry does not stem only from absent information. It can be produced by special languages that function as barriers of competence. The consumer receives the text, but does not receive real access to the code that organizes its meaning. Technical, legal and business language has a social function of distinction and exclusion. It communicates to the initiated and, at the same time, reaffirms the position of those who master the code. In practical terms, this means that the mere making available of terms, policies or notices does not eliminate semiotic exclusion when full understanding remains reserved to those who master the grammar of the system<1><2>685</2></1>. The difficulty, then, is not episodic. It is structural. The consumer does not merely get one datum wrong. He adheres within a frame of language that already places him outside the center of intelligibility of the relation.

It is at this point that one can speak of meaning-vitiated consent. It is not a matter of a one-off factual error, such as confusing a price or an isolated deadline. It is a matter of an inability, <1>p. 604</1> structurally produced by the communicational conditions of supply, to decode, compare and anticipate relevant consequences. Submission stems not only from express omission, but from an architecture of language, interface and framing that conditions in advance access to the legal and economic meaning of the decision. The consumer may be formally informed and, even so, materially cut off from the meaning of what he accepts. This is the communicational form of semiotic vulnerability.

On the plane of the CDC, this brings the problem back to the duty to inform in its material sense. The supplier does not fulfill this duty merely because it made the content technically accessible by click, scrolling or download. What matters is whether the average consumer could read and understand what those clauses meant, which rights and obligations were being assumed and which practical consequences followed from adhesion. The mere mention of the existence of general conditions is not enough when the meaning remains opaque<1><2>686</2></1>. The principle of transparency, in this picture, is not a peripheral formality. It affects the very essence of the transaction, because information is part of the content of the contract and, if it fails, compromises the legal quality of the performance.

This explains why contractual obscurity, in consumption, is not an innocent stylistic flaw. It is evidence of structural disloyalty in the organization of consent. In adhesion contracts, the consumer does not take part in the drafting and enters the relation trusting that there is a minimum of textual intelligibility and loyalty. For this reason, the control of these clauses is not limited to a neutral grammatical examination, but is guided by objective good faith and by the protection of the adherent's trust. Pre-drafted clauses must be read so as to respect the legitimate interests of those who accepted them without being able to negotiate them, and obscure drafting triggers precisely the presumption that the supplier failed in the duty to organize consent on loyal bases<1><2>687</2></1>.

<1>p. 605</1> This asymmetric communicational regime also helps to explain why semiotic vulnerability is not to be confused with a loose cultural metaphor. It describes a real disadvantage of decoding, comparison and resistance produced by the way the market organizes its language. In IOCs, this is amplified because the supplier's communication is not limited to the written contract. It projects itself onto showcases, in-game stores, purchase screens, event messages, update announcements, metrics, rankings, signals of rarity and framings of value that are part of the consumption experience. The consumer faces not just a text. He faces an entire grammar of governed enjoyment.

The dogmatic consequence is twofold. First, the duty to inform must be read as a duty of intelligibility, adequacy and verifiability, and not as a mere delivery of documentary volume. Second, consumer protection in platform environments requires <1>standards</1> capable of simultaneously reducing the asymmetry of meaning and the asymmetry of evidence. If the platform controls the language through which the object is presented, understood and accepted, it also tends to control the records, framings and traces through which adhesion and frustration may later be reconstructed. For this reason, language, code and consent are not a peripheral theme. They are one of the bases on which, in what follows, requirements of open auditability and criteria of restoration by functional value equivalence are justified.

“Art. 31. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information, in the Portuguese language, about their characteristics, qualities, quantity, composition, price, warranty, expiry dates and origin, among other data, as well as about the risks they pose to the health and safety of consumers.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>

Legal and institutional language is not neutral, operating as a technique of production and stabilization of meaning immersed in political and strategic factors, which rules out the image of the contract or interface as mere transparent containers of information. Pragmatics applied to law makes it possible to perceive that ideology is “a factor inseparable from the conceptual structure made explicit in general norms”, requiring of the interpreter a reading that discovers “the connections between the words of the law and the political and ideological factors that produce and determine their functions in society” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</2>. Legal language, thus, does not merely inform; it organizes possible intelligibilities and blocks others. This finding is crucial for understanding how the consumer's consent can be vitiated by structurally produced meaning, and not merely by a one-off absence of data. Normative discourses involve a “game of persuasion and mythification” that stereotypes meanings and legitimizes the reproduction of power under an appearance of normality <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 45)</4>. Through the use of “a language impregnated with stereotyped significations”, there is introduced, “under the supposed appearance of an objective description, an ideological dimension not formulated in legal language”, the central objective of these expressions being “to influence and determine opinions” <5>Warat</5><6>(Warat, 1984, p. 71)</6>. In consequence, the consumer may perfectly well receive the text, click, accept and even repeat its terms without ever reaching its real practical intelligibility, because communicational subjection does not depend only on the lack of access to the statement, but on the selective and asymmetric way in which meaning is produced for him. <7>↩</7>

Normative, contractual and regulatory texts produce selective intelligibility and can organize forms of communicational subjection, since the very coherent organization of discourse functions as a filtering mechanism that silences problems and excludes uncomfortable readings. The “coherent organization of a discourse” can “silence problems” and, through these silences, fulfill “political functions in society”, at the same time as it “explicitly forces subjects to say or repress certain things” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 50)</2>. Intelligibility, thus, is not distributed neutrally; it is selectively produced. This selectivity is reinforced when legal discourse presents itself under the appearance of univocity and closure: the belief in normative univocity presupposes “prior ideological coincidence” and the unalterability of signifiers sustains the ideal of a rational norm precisely because it ensures certain “social effects of the law in society” <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 68)</4>. In criticizing the assertion of the closed character of legal language, it becomes evident that the demands of totality and closure of the system are not mere logical requirements, but ideological representations that satisfy specific functions of the legal form <5>Warat</5><6>(Warat, 1984, p. 54)</6>. In consequence, institutional texts can organize communicational subjection not only through what they expressly say, but through the way they stabilize meanings, exclude interpretive alternatives and induce adherence to a previously controlled semantic frame. The acceptance of rules, framings and institutional conditions can be produced discursively without the need for an explicit command, through a “discursive work” that manipulates words and stereotypes to fabricate acceptance and naturalize authority. The consensus on the legitimacy of power is the result of a discursive work, which is effective precisely because it operates through “a game of stereotyping”, whose primary function is legitimation <7>Warat</7><8>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</8>. Power produces meanings that make adherence seem spontaneous, reasonable or inevitable, constituting an “ordered subjectivity”, shaped by the “social idiom” and progressively alienated from the ends of the power that shapes it. In this situation, physical violence becomes largely dispensable, being replaced by “significant violence” and “imaginary violence”, capable of neutralizing the critical potency of subjectivity and producing internalized obedience <9>Warat</9><10>(Warat, 1984, p. 110)</10>. Certain effects of acceptance propagate without the need for explicit demonstration, relying on stereotypes, topical formulas and already sedimented beliefs, so that discursive alignment spreads “like an infection” or “contagion” <11>Warat</11><12>(Warat, 1984, p. 88)</12>. Communicational subjection, therefore, does not depend only on what is said imperatively, but on the production of a horizon of meaning in which obeying, adhering or accepting comes to seem simply the normal course of things. <13>↩</13>

The fragility of consent, in contractual environments mediated by platforms, stems not only from the absence of information, but also from the organization of a functionally exclusionary language, which allows the formal receipt of the message without ensuring effective access to its meaning. The problem, thus, is not reduced to the episodic lack of a given datum, but involves a structural asymmetry of intelligibility: the consumer comes into contact with text, interface and contracting commands, but remains outside the code that organizes the real legal meaning of the operation. It is at this point that Gnerre offers direct support, by demonstrating that certain specialized languages serve not only to communicate, but also to distinguish and exclude. As the author states, "the central function of all special languages is social: they have a real communicative value but they exclude from communication the people of the linguistic community external to the group that uses the special language and, on the other hand, they have the function of reaffirming the identity of the members of the reduced group that has access to the special language." <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 23)</2>. The mere making available of terms, policies or notices, therefore, does not eliminate semiotic exclusion when full understanding remains reserved to those initiated in the technical, business or legal code of the relation. In a convergent sense, Gnerre observes that "language constitutes the most powerful barbed wire for blocking access to power", adding that, to draft a document with legal value, it is not enough to know the language in the ordinary sense, it being necessary to master "a whole complex and archaizing phraseology that is customary" <3>Gnerre</3><4>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 22)</4>. Transposed to digital consumption, this shows that the defect of consent may emerge not only from the concealment of information, but from the very structural withholding of meaning. <5>↩</5>

Within the CDC, the duty to inform is not satisfied by the mere formal making available of content nor by the mere physical existence of clauses accessible by click, scrolling or abstractly possible reading. It is a material duty of clarity and understanding, aimed at ensuring that the consumer has effective access to the legal and practical meaning of what is presented to him as the basis of consent. Communicational asymmetry, therefore, is not resolved by proof that the text was "there", but by the assessment that its content was knowable in real terms for the average consumer, especially in contexts of strong unilateral predisposition: "the mere mention that CONDGs will be used in the contract is not enough, it is necessary that the ordinary man can read and understand what those clauses mean, which obligations and rights he is accepting" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 91-92)</2>. The exclusion of intelligibility compromises the legitimacy of consent because it affects the very material content of the legally owed information, in conflict with objective good faith and with the protection of trust. The principle of transparency governs the pre-contractual moment and the very conclusion of the contract, being "more than a mere formal element", since it "affects the essence of the transaction", as information "is part of the content of the contract or, if it fails, represents a failure in the quality of the product or service offered" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 819)</4>. Obscure texts and communicational architectures that deliver words while withholding meaning produce a zone of materially vitiated consent. <5>↩</5>

The control of adhesion contracts and of obscure drafting, in the CDC system, is not limited to a neutral grammatical examination, but is guided by objective good faith and by the protection of the consumer's trust in light of contractual justice and the legitimate expectations of the adherent. In pre-drafted clauses, the consumer does not take part in the formulation of the text and frequently enters the relation trusting that the drafting respects a minimum of loyalty and intelligibility. For this reason, the new function of contract law places back in a central position the principle of interpretation in accordance with good faith, so that art. 47 of the CDC, together with the general clause of art. 51, IV, allows pre-drafted clauses to be interpreted "in a way that respects the trust and the legitimate interests of the consumers who accepted these pre-drafted clauses" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 94-95)</2>. Obscurity is not an aesthetic flaw, but evidence of structural disloyalty in the organization of consent. Breach of the duty of clear drafting finds its sanction in art. 46 of the CDC, according to which contracts do not bind the consumer if they are drafted in a way that hinders the understanding of their meaning and scope, a sanction that originates in the "presumption of bad faith of the supplier-drafter of the contract" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 902-903)</4>. An incomprehensible clause is not proof of robust consent; it is a symptom of betrayed trust with a drafting varnish. <5>↩</5>

Semiotic vulnerability only gains dogmatic usefulness when it ceases to function as a general diagnosis of the environment and begins to operate as a scheme of attribution and control. In IOCs, this requires disciplining three distinct and articulated planes: the mechanism alleged, the objective basis by which this mechanism can be demonstrated and the typical consequence that the CDC already allows to be drawn from it. The point is not to assert, impressionistically, that the consumer was “manipulated” or “confused”. The point is to show that the communicational regime of supply was structured so as to produce a relevant asymmetry of <1>p. 606</1> understanding, comparison and contestation, and that this asymmetry can be brought back to legally controllable duties, defects and remedies.

On the first plane, what is alleged is not a failure to read, individual distraction or psychological incapacity of the consumer. The allegation falls on a communicational and architectural structure that distributes power. In IOCs, the platform controls language, framings, signals of equivalence, criteria of rarity, acceptance flows, update messages and forms of visibility of the object itself. This means that it not only informs about enjoyment, but administers the means by which enjoyment will be perceived and evaluated. The asymmetry, therefore, does not arise from a subjective deficiency of the user, but from an unequal distribution of communicational competence and of the power to define meaning<1><2>688</2></1>. For this reason, semiotic vulnerability can be alleged as a legal fact: the supplier organizes in advance the field of what can be understood, compared and accepted.

This structure is aggravated because, in IOC ecosystems, the governance of meaning is continuous. The platform does not limit itself to communicating once, at the moment of contracting. It permanently reorganizes the decision environment and the enjoyment environment. The legally relevant allegation, then, can take stable forms. It may consist of informational inadequacy, when the information exists but does not guide a useful decision. It may consist of a breach of good faith, when the architecture of the environment hinders the formation of free and rational will. It may consist of objective disloyalty, when relevant changes are communicated in a ritualized, dispersed manner or at an inadequate moment. And it may consist of improper management of expectation, when offer, interface and decision flow are organized to produce an asymmetric perception of advantage, risk or equivalence. It is precisely at this level that the category leaves the abstract plane and enters the real CDC, because the transparency required by the system <1>p. 607</1> does not mean the mere formal existence of texts, but respect for the normal interests of the consumer and the organization of material conditions for a considered decision<2><3>689</3></2>.

On the second plane, operationalization requires shifting the evidence from impressionistic ground to the communicational and architectural materiality of supply. The object of proof is not the inner state of the consumer considered in isolation. What is proven is the objective form of the decision path and of the enjoyment regime as structured by the platform. This allows semiotic vulnerability to be reconstructed through external, replicable and institutionally controllable elements. The first source of support is interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade and confirmation screens, messages about rarity, equivalence, time remaining, discount, event or change. What is relevant there is not the user's subjective memory, but the architecture actually presented. The allegation ceases to be “I did not understand” and becomes “the environment was designed this way”.

The second source of support is the history of the offer and of mutability. The advertising and institutional promise is compared with the enjoyment actually delivered and with its later changes. What is sought to be shown is not generic subjective frustration, but possible relevant degradation, loss of functional equivalence or unilateral reconfiguration with material impact on the experience. In IOCs, this comparison is central because the object is not exhausted in its nominal existence. Its legal character depends on the maintenance of enjoyment in functionally recognizable terms. Proving the change of the environment, of the utility, of the comparability or of the intelligibility of the experience is proving a change of the supply regime itself.

The third source of support falls on advertising and its identifying documents. Promotional pieces, posts, campaigns, influencers, disclaimers, asterisks, cascading cross-references and fine print serve to map how the expectation was produced and where the <1>p. 608</1> relevant conditions were hidden, diluted or moved to zones of low visibility. The same applies to proof of informational noise. Excess becomes opacity when there is fragmentation, circular cross-references, indecipherable technical language, internal contradictions, detachment between information and the moment of decision or displacement of the essential away from the point of choice. The evidentiary core is not to demonstrate the absence of text, but the structural inadequacy of the communication for purposes of useful understanding.

This evidentiary model also requires recognizing that semiotic asymmetry projects itself into an asymmetry of evidence. Whoever controls the service controls, to a large extent, the decisive records of the relation. <1>Logs</1>, version histories, transactions, interface parameters, change communications and relevant technical documentation tend to remain in the supplier's possession. For this reason, the operationalization of the category must be accompanied by requests for preservation and production of minimum documentation of the supply. Without this, the consumer is prevented from demonstrating precisely what the IOC regime makes central. This is not a procedural favor. It is a matter of neutralizing the private concentration of the means of reconstructing the case. The CDC's language for this response already exists. Consumer protection admits rebalancing techniques when the informational failure and the form of the bond reveal a material defect in the formation or performance of the relation<2><3>690</3></2>.

On the third plane, semiotic vulnerability must lead to foreseeable consequences. The first group is informational. If the problem is the decisional inadequacy of the communication, the request cannot simply be “more information”. The remedy is qualified information, organized in a clear, adequate and verifiable way at the moment of decision. This may mean conspicuous highlighting of the essential, reorganization of the communication flow, prohibition of obscure cross-references or the requirement of materially useful notice about relevant changes. The second group is that of control of the offer and of practices. When the legitimate expectation was produced by ambiguity, relevant omission or semiotic management of the perception of value, correction, inhibition and restoration of the frustration produced are appropriate.

<1>p. 609</1> The third group is that of the ineffectiveness of obscurity. Clauses, internal rules, cascading terms and ritual acceptances that operate as semiotic traps should not be treated as a robust manifestation of consent. When language hinders real understanding of the meaning and scope of adhesion, the consumer-law system already authorizes neutralizing the effectiveness of obscurity in the concrete case. The fourth group is evidentiary. In the face of the concentration of records, preservation and production of the trails of supply are appropriate, with a rational redistribution of the burden and presumptions favorable to the consumer when the supplier does not cooperate or keeps the evidence in a black box.

This scheme shows that semiotic vulnerability is not a decorative concept. It organizes allegation, evidence and request. What is alleged is a structural asymmetry of meaning produced by the supply regime. What is proven is the communicational and architectural materiality of that asymmetry. What is requested is the correction of the decision environment, the neutralization of obscurity, the production of records and the restoration of the affected enjoyment. The category thus ceases to be a theoretical label and comes to function as an operator. It is precisely this that prepares the passage to open auditability and to the qualification of abusive teleology as a defect of the supply regime itself. Warat helps to recall only the core of the mechanism being converted into a legal allegation: the problem lies not in an inner deficiency of the consumer, but in a structure of language and framing that unequally takes from him the power to constitute the meaning of his own relation<1><2>691</2></1>.

The operationalization of semiotic vulnerability does not start from the idea of the consumer's individual inattention, but from the recognition of an unequal distribution of legally relevant communicational competence. The problem is not to censure the user for not having read or understood everything, but to identify that contractual and operational communication was structured according to codes, references and forms of expression whose full apprehension is not equally distributed among the participants in the consumer relation. At this point, Gnerre functions as a subsidiary reinforcement in recalling that the linguistic registers of greatest prestige and power are not universally accessible. As the author observes, "only a part of the members of complex societies, for example, has access to a 'cultivated' or 'standard variety, generally considered 'the language', and typically associated with contents of prestige. The standard language is a communicative system within reach of a reduced part of the members of a community" <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 6)</2>. The same mechanism appears when the platform adjusts syntax, lexicon and frame of references so as to restrict the effective addressees of the message, since, as the author adds, "to reduce or broaden the range of the possible receivers of political and cultural messages it is enough to adjust the syntax, the frame of references and the lexicon" <3>Gnerre</3><4>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 21)</4>. In IOCs, this reinforces that semiotic vulnerability concerns the very communicational architecture of supply, and not a psychological failure or mere negligence in reading. <5>↩</5>

The operationalization of semiotic vulnerability, in the sphere of IOCs, requires bringing it back to the concrete decision plane of the CDC, that is, to the ground on which the asymmetry of meaning is converted into legally relevant informational inadequacy, breach of objective good faith and grounds for requests to correct the supply regime itself. Marques offers decisive support in stating that good faith, made concrete in the consumer relation, "means mandatory transparency toward the contractual partner, a mandatory respect for the normal interests of the other contracting party, a positive action by the stronger contractual partner to allow the weaker contractual partner the conditions necessary for the formation of a free and rational will", adding that ensuring information, protection against the pressures of sales methods and time for reflection are legal objectives of this pursuit of a rational decision by the consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812)</2>. In a convergent sense, the author argues that the possibility of prior knowledge of the contractual text and of the obligations it contains is an "essential condition for the formation of a truly free, conscious, 'rational will", which is why art. 46 allows the consumer to request in court release from the bond due to a failure of the supplier's duties of information <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 898-899)</4>. This allows semiotic vulnerability to be translated into allegation, evidence and request within the real CDC. <5>↩</5>

The CDC does not limit itself to recognizing, in theory, that the consumer's freedom of choice may be compromised by inadequate contractual and informational structures; it provides for concrete corrective consequences precisely to rebalance the decision environment when the formation of will proves materially defective. Marques formulates this reasoning by stating that, in the face of the structural "pressures" that unbalance contracting in consumer society, there arises the need for a "rebalancing legal response", exemplified by control of the content of the contract, by "a new informative formalism" and by the right of withdrawal without cause, all this "with the aim of rebalancing or supplying the 'factual failure' in the freedom or will of the weaker contracting party." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 287)</2>. The author also highlights the case-law tendency to declare the ineffectiveness of contractual clauses and even of entire consumer bonds on the basis of arts. 46 and 54, § 4, of the CDC, precisely because of problems of form and contractual drafting revealing insufficient information and warning to the consumer <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1304)</4>. This authorizes structuring corrective requests aimed not only at later reparation, but at the refinement of the supply regime itself. <5>↩</5>

Warat offers a bridge for bringing back the mechanism underlying semiotic vulnerability. The relevant asymmetry is not founded on a psychological incapacity of the consumer, but on an unequal distribution of power through language, communicational framing and ritualization of meaning. The author warns that the function of domination should not be analyzed “from a psychologistic point of view”, since senders and receivers are institutionally situated and their discourses operate as supports of a mediatized ideology <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 67)</2>. The inequality, therefore, lies not in a supposed subjective deficiency of the addressee, but in the way the communicational structure is organized in advance to favor certain poles of definition, interpretation and legitimation. This key is reinforced when Warat shows that the producer of discourse can secure for himself “the monopoly of the constitution of the denotative field”, selecting designative properties for persuasive purposes and leaving the receivers “asleep to the discussion of the persuasively proposed designative criteria” <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 70)</4>. It is precisely this kind of communicational disciplining, and not an inner failure of the consumer, that can be brought back to the legal allegation of semiotic vulnerability in IOCs. <5>↩</5>
